entry: Chemical bond formed by the sharing of [[Electron|electron]] pairs between [[Atom|atoms]]. In a covalent bond the shared pairs, also called bonding pairs, give each atom the equivalent of a full valence shell, a stable electronic configuration. Covalent bonding is much more common than [[Ionic bonding|ionic bonding]] in [[Organic chemistry|organic chemistry]], where atoms are merely held together by electrostatic attraction. The term "covalence" was introduced by [[Irving Langmuir|Irving Langmuir]] in 1919, and [[Gilbert N. Lewis|Gilbert N. Lewis]] described shared electron pairs in 1916. In the molecule H₂, the two [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] atoms share two electrons. Walter Heitler and Fritz London gave the first [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanical]] explanation of a chemical bond, in molecular hydrogen, in 1927. Covalent character is greatest between atoms with similar electronegativities. Electrons shared among more than two atoms are called delocalized.

Measure of the joint variability of two [[Random variable|random variables]]. Covariance is positive when the variables tend to show similar behavior and negative when they tend to show opposite behavior. Its magnitude reflects the geometric mean of the [[Variance|variances]] shared by the two variables, so a larger magnitude indicates stronger mutual dependence. Its units are those of X times those of Y, so changing the units changes its value proportionally, which makes strength hard to judge from covariance alone. The [[Correlation|correlation coefficient]] normalizes covariance to a value between −1 and 1 by dividing by the product of the [[Standard deviation|standard deviations]]. For jointly distributed variables X and Y, covariance is the [[Expected value|expected value]] of the product of their deviations from their means: cov(X,Y) = E[(X − E[X])(Y − E[Y])]. Covariance is zero for independent variables, though the converse does not hold.

Cathedral city and metropolitan borough in the West Midlands, [[England|England]] (pop., 2021: 345,324). Coventry's city status was formally recognized in a charter of 1345, and it was a wealthy centre in the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]]. In the 19th century it developed a large [[Bicycle|bicycle]] industry, and in the 20th it became a major centre of the British motor industry. German air raids in November 1940 destroyed much of the historic city centre. The city was rebuilt after the Second World War. It was named UK City of Culture for 2021.

Japanese neo-noir space [[Western (genre)|Western]] [[Anime|anime]] television series, broadcast 1998–99. Created and animated by Sunrise, the 26-episode series is set in 2071 and follows bounty hunters aboard the spaceship Bebop. It draws most heavily on [[Science fiction|science fiction]], Western and noir films, and explores themes of existential [[Boredom|boredom]] and [[Loneliness|loneliness]]. Its English dub is regarded as one of the best anime dubs. It is credited with helping introduce anime to a new wave of Western viewers in the early 2000s.

Canine species native to North America (*Canis latrans*), also known as the American jackal and prairie wolf. The coyote is smaller than the gray [[Wolf|wolf]] and fills much of the same ecological niche as the [[Golden jackal|golden jackal]] in Eurasia. Listed as least concern by the IUCN, it adapts readily to human-modified environments, and urban coyotes are common in many cities. Adult males average 8 to 20 kg and females 7 to 18 kg. Its diet is mainly [[Deer|deer]], [[Rabbit|rabbits]], hares, [[Rodent|rodents]], birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish and invertebrates. Humans are its greatest threat, followed by [[Cougar|cougars]] and gray wolves. Coyotes interbreed with eastern and red wolves to produce "coywolf" [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]], and the species has 19 recognized subspecies.

Mythological character common to many Indigenous cultures of North America. He is usually male and anthropomorphic, though he may have coyote features such as fur, pointed ears and a tail. [[Myth|Myths]] about him vary widely, and his role shares some traits with the Raven figure in other cultures. In [[Navajo|Navajo]] tradition, Coyote is the tutelary spirit of the Coyoteway curing ceremony, which is meant to restore the patient's harmony with Coyote and the world. In many California stories he is a sacred creator with divine powers; in others he is a malevolent, comical trickster. A common theme is Coyote obtaining fire or the sun from supernatural beings for the benefit of people. In a Maidu myth, Coyote and Earth Maker sing the world into being, after which Coyote vows to spoil it and introduce evil. Some stories depict him as a lecherous figure whose outrageous humor may have reinforced community moral codes.

[[Supernova|Supernova]] remnant and [[Pulsar|pulsar]] wind nebula in the constellation [[Taurus (constellation)|Taurus]], about 6,500 light-years from Earth. It corresponds to a bright supernova observed in AD 1054 by Chinese, Japanese and Arab astronomers, and it was the first astronomical object identified with a historically observed supernova. English astronomer John Bevis discovered it in 1731. Charles Messier rediscovered it in 1758 while searching for a [[Comet|comet]] and made it the first entry in his catalogue. The nebula is about 11 light-years across and expands at about 1,500 km per second. Its [[Apparent magnitude|apparent magnitude]] of 8.4 makes it visible with [[Binoculars|binoculars]] under favourable conditions. At its center lies the Crab Pulsar, a [[Neutron star|neutron star]] that spins 30.2 times per second and emits radiation from gamma rays to radio waves. At X-ray and [[Gamma ray|gamma-ray]] energies above 30 keV, the nebula is generally the brightest persistent gamma-ray source in the sky.

[[Decapod|Decapod]] [[Crustacean|crustacean]] with a heavily armoured shell, its tail tucked under the body, and a sideways gait. Crabs are not a single natural group. The crab form, produced by a process called carcinisation, evolved independently several times, including in the [[Brachyura|true crabs]] and in the Anomura, which include hermit crabs and porcelain crabs. Sizes range from the pea crab, a few millimeters wide, to the [[Japanese spider crab|Japanese spider crab]], with a leg span up to 4 m. Crabs make up about 20% of marine crustaceans caught or farmed for human consumption. Hermit crabs are often kept in [[Aquarium|aquariums]].

Location and culture from which one of the earliest [[Civilization|human civilizations]] emerged independently. A civilization is a complex society marked by a state, social stratification, [[Urbanization|urbanization]], and [[Writing system|writing systems]] or graphic arts. Scholars generally acknowledge six cradles: [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], ancient India and ancient China in Afro-Eurasia, and the [[Caral–Supe civilization|Caral–Supe civilization]] of coastal Peru and the Olmec civilization of Mexico in the Americas. All depended on [[Agriculture|agriculture]], except possibly Caral–Supe, which may have relied initially on marine resources. By the 31st century BC, [[Uruk|Uruk]], Ur, Kish and Eridu in Mesopotamia, followed by Susa and Memphis, had grown to several tens of thousands of inhabitants. Proto-writing appeared at Harappa in the Indus Valley around 3,300 BC.

Group of evergreen dwarf shrubs and trailing vines in the genus *Vaccinium*, bearing tart, edible [[Berry (botany)|berries]]. The low, creeping plants have slender stems, small evergreen leaves and dark pink flowers, which are pollinated by bees. The berry starts light green, turns red when ripe, and its acidity usually overwhelms its sweetness. Cranberries grow in acidic [[Bog|bogs]] across the cooler Northern Hemisphere. German and Dutch colonists in New England, around 1694, named the fruit for the resemblance of the flower to a [[Crane (bird)|crane]]'s neck, head and bill. Henry Hall, a veteran of the [[American Revolutionary War|American Revolutionary War]], first cultivated cranberries in Dennis, on [[Cape Cod|Cape Cod]], around 1816. In 2020 the United States, Canada and Chile produced 97% of world output. Cranberry sauce is a traditional accompaniment to turkey at [[Thanksgiving|Thanksgiving]] dinners in the U.S. and Canada. In 2021 U.S. output was 360,000 metric tons, 59% of it from [[Wisconsin|Wisconsin]].

Large, long-legged, long-necked [[Bird|bird]] of the family Gruidae, order [[Gruiformes|Gruiformes]]. The family has 15 living species in four genera: *Antigone*, *Balearica*, *Leucogeranus* and *Grus*. Cranes fly with their necks and legs outstretched, unlike [[Heron|herons]], which bend their necks into an S-shape. Most species are gray or white, but the crowned cranes of *Balearica* have brightly colored wings and golden crowns of feathers. Cranes live on most continents except [[Antarctica|Antarctica]] and [[South America|South America]]. They breed in pairs but form large flocks outside the breeding season. Both parents rear the young, which stay with them until the next breeding season. Most species are classed as at least threatened. The plight of the whooping crane in North America inspired some of the first U.S. laws protecting endangered species.

Fly of the dipteran superfamily Tipuloidea, with a slender body and long, stilt-like legs that are easily detached. The superfamily includes four living families: Cylindrotomidae, Limoniidae, Pediciidae and Tipulidae. More than 15,500 species in over 500 genera have been described, most of them by C.P. Alexander. Crane flies first appeared in the Middle Triassic, around 245 million years ago. They are most diverse in the [[Tropics|tropics]] but occur worldwide. Adults generally do not feed. Their [[Larva|larvae]], called leatherjackets, usually feed on decaying plant matter, though some species eat living plants, fungi or other invertebrates. In colloquial speech they are sometimes called "daddy longlegs," a name also used for [[Arachnid|arachnids]].

Lifting machine with a boom, hoist and wire ropes or chains, used to move heavy loads. The first known crane was the shaduf, a water-lifting device invented in [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] and later used in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]]. Greek construction cranes were powered by men or animals, and the [[Roman Empire|Roman]] Empire developed larger cranes operated by human treadwheels. In the High Middle Ages, harbour cranes loaded and unloaded ships. Cranes were built of wood until cast iron, iron and steel took over during the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]]. The first mechanical power came from [[Steam engine|steam engines]], and modern cranes use [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engines]] or electric motors with hydraulic systems. Types range from workshop jib cranes to tower cranes for high-rise buildings, and large floating cranes that build oil rigs and salvage sunken ships. The name comes from the resemblance of the machine to the long neck of the [[Crane (bird)|bird]].

Freshwater [[Crustacean|crustacean]] of the infraorder Astacidea, related to [[Lobster|lobsters]]. Crayfish, also called crawfish or crawdads, comprise over 640 species in the superfamilies Astacoidea of the Northern Hemisphere and Parastacoidea of the Southern Hemisphere. They breathe through feather-like [[Gill|gills]] and live in brooks, streams, [[Swamp|swamps]], ditches and paddy fields. Most cannot tolerate polluted water, although *Procambarus clarkii* is hardier. Crayfish are opportunistic omnivores that feed mostly on mud and detritus at the sediment surface, along with plants and animals. The invasive red swamp crayfish and rusty crayfish outcompete native species outside their native ranges. Crayfish are farmed in [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]] industries, notably in China and [[Louisiana|Louisiana]].

Dairy product composed of the higher-fat layer skimmed from the top of [[Milk|milk]]. Cream is graded by butterfat content, from light to heavy, and contains high levels of saturated fat. Cream skimmed from whey, a by-product of [[Cheese|cheese]]-making, has less fat and a saltier, tangier taste. Partially fermented cream is sold as sour cream and *crème fraîche*. Cream from [[Cattle|cattle]] grazing on pasture, particularly Jersey cattle, is often yellowish from carotenoid pigments, while cream from [[Goat|goat]] or [[Water buffalo|water buffalo]] milk, or from cows fed indoors on grain, is white. Cream is used in [[Ice cream|ice cream]], sauces, soups, puddings and cakes, and whipped cream tops [[Pie|pies]] and [[Peach|peaches]]. In France, food products labeled "cream" must contain at least 12% milk fat under a decree of April 23, 1980.

Type of cosmogony, a symbolic narrative of how the world began and how humans first came to inhabit it. Creation myths are found in nearly all known [[Religion|religious]] traditions and are usually regarded as conveying profound truths, metaphorically, symbolically, historically or literally. Their characters are deities, human-like figures or animals, set in a dim past that religion historian Mircea Eliade called *in illo tempore* ("at that time"). Over 100 distinct ones have been discovered. Most are etiological, attempting to explain how the world formed and where humanity came from, and they reveal the central [[Worldview|worldview]] of the culture that tells them. Because they develop in [[Oral tradition|oral traditions]], they typically exist in multiple versions.

American [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit organization]] that publishes free [[Copyright|copyright]] licenses. Founded in 2001 by Lawrence Lessig, Hal Abelson and Eric Eldred, it released its first licenses in December 2002. The licenses let creators state which rights they reserve and which they waive, replacing individual negotiation under "all rights reserved" copyright. As of 2019 there were "nearly 2 billion" works under them, including [[Wikipedia|Wikipedia]] and its sister projects. Critics argue that the licenses may reduce incentives for original creation through uncompensated reuse.

Ability to generate novel and valuable ideas or works through the exercise of [[Imagination|imagination]]. Creative products may be intangible, such as ideas, scientific theories, literary works, musical compositions and jokes, or physical, such as [[Invention|inventions]], meals, jewelry, [[Costume|costumes]] and [[Painting|paintings]]. Creativity also enables people to find new solutions to problems. Most ancient cultures, including those of [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], China and India, lacked the concept and saw art as discovery rather than creation; the modern conception emerged during the [[Renaissance|Renaissance]]. Psychology professor Michael Mumford wrote that there is general agreement that creativity involves "the production of novel, useful products." Creativity is usually distinguished from innovation, which emphasizes implementation. Scholarly interest is found mainly in [[Psychology|psychology]], business studies and cognitive science.

Payment card, usually issued by a [[Bank|bank]], for purchases or cash withdrawals on credit. Unlike a [[Debit card|debit card]], it allows a continuing balance subject to [[Interest (economics)|interest]], so the holder accrues [[Debt|debt]]. A charge card instead requires the full balance to be repaid each month. The first general-purpose charge card was introduced by Diners Club in 1950, which required the entire bill to be paid each statement. [[Bank of America|Bank of America]]'s BankAmericard, launched in 1958, later evolved into Visa. In June 2018 there were 7.75 billion credit cards worldwide. In 2020, 1.09 billion were in circulation in the [[United States|United States]], held by 72.5% of adults. Some studies find that card users spend more, and critics argue that high-interest revolving balances contribute to financial distress.

Statement of the shared beliefs of a community, often religious, that summarizes its core tenets. The term derives from Latin *credo*, "I believe," the opening word of the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed. Many [[Christian denomination|Christian denominations]] use three creeds: the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, the Apostles' Creed and the Athanasian Creed, while some use none. The [[Nicene Creed|Nicene Creed]] was first formulated in AD 325 at the [[First Council of Nicaea|First Council of Nicaea]] to affirm the deity of Christ, and it was revised in AD 381 to affirm the [[Trinity|Trinity]] as a whole. It was historically used against [[Arianism|Arianism]]. The Apostles' Creed, which is widely used in Western church services, concisely summarizes the virgin birth, crucifixion and resurrection. In [[Islam|Islam]], the closest concept is *ʿaqīdah* ("bond, tie").

American [[Rock music|rock]] band formed in El Cerrito, California, in 1968. Its members had played together since 1959 as the Blue Velvets and the Golliwogs. Led by John Fogerty, the band had 14 consecutive top-10 singles and five consecutive top-10 albums in the United States between 1969 and 1971. It performed at [[Woodstock|Woodstock]] in 1969. The band broke up acrimoniously in 1972 amid lawsuits among its members. The compilation *Chronicle: The 20 Greatest Hits*, released in 1976, has been certified 12-times platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America.

Method of final disposition of a corpse by burning, as a funeral rite or an alternative to burial. In modern times cremation is usually carried out in a closed furnace, or cremator, at a crematorium; in [[India|India]] and [[Nepal|Nepal]], open-air pyres remain an ancient tradition. Cremation dates from at least 17,000 years ago, when the remains of a partly cremated body, the Mungo Lady, were found at Lake Mungo, Australia. Cremation was common but not universal in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] and [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]], and it declined in Europe with the rise of [[Christianity|Christianity]]. [[Hinduism|Hinduism]] and [[Jainism|Jainism]] prescribe it. Cremation became widespread again in the 19th century, and the U.S. cremation rate reached 61.8% in 2024. An average of 2.4 kg of remains, called ashes or cremains, is left; these are inert and pose no health risk.

Stable language that develops from the mixing and simplification of parent languages. Creoles are distinguished from pidgins by a consistent grammar, a large stable vocabulary, and native speakers who acquire them as a first language. About one hundred creole languages have arisen since 1500, mostly based on European languages such as English and French, because of colonization and the [[Atlantic slave trade|Atlantic slave trade]]. Many arose during the [[Age of Discovery|Age of Discovery]]. Their lexicon comes largely from the parent languages, particularly the dominant group's, though grammars often develop new features. A creole is believed to arise when a pidgin becomes the native language of children, a process called nativization. Creolistics, a subfield of [[Linguistics|linguistics]], studies them. Many creoles from European colonies were stigmatized and became extinct, but some now have official status. Creoles based on [[Arabic|Arabic]], Chinese and Malay also exist.

Category of carbonaceous chemicals produced by [[Distillation|distilling]] [[Tar|tars]] or by heating plant material such as wood. Coal-tar creosote, the main industrial form, is a wood preservative used for railroad ties, utility poles and marine pilings. It is applied by pressure under licensed supervision, and it is more toxic than wood-tar creosote, which was used to preserve meat and as a medical antiseptic. Creosotes give smoked meat its characteristic flavor and scent; the name comes from Greek for "meat" and "preserver." Its toxicity and environmental effects have prompted regulatory restrictions in some regions; the U.S. EPA classes it as a [[Pesticide|pesticide]] for wood preservation.

Geological boundary marked by a thin band of iridium-rich rock, dated to 66.043 ± 0.043 million years ago. It marks the end of the [[Cretaceous|Cretaceous]] Period and the start of the [[Paleogene|Paleogene]] Period. It coincides with the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]], which destroyed most Mesozoic species, including all non-avian [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]]. The generally accepted view is that an [[Asteroid|asteroid]] impact formed the [[Chicxulub crater|Chicxulub crater]] beneath the [[Yucatán Peninsula|Yucatán Peninsula]] in [[Mexico|Mexico]] and triggered the extinction. The crater is over 150 km in diameter.
